title: Public, internal, confidential: how our data classification works

audience.who: Corporate employees in any role who create, store and share documents, files and messages every day
audience.knows: That some information is sensitive; not the three class names, what goes in each, or what each class lets them do
audience.cares_about: Sharing quickly without getting it wrong, not being the person who caused a leak, knowing what to do when unsure

outcome: Given an everyday document, file or message, the viewer can put it in public, internal or confidential and handle it the way that class requires, and knows what to do when unsure.
through_line: Every piece of information already has a class; deciding it takes one question about who could be harmed if it got out, and the class then tells you how to handle it.

arc_plan.what: A familiar moment: about to send or post a file and pausing, not sure who is allowed to see it
Three classes, one question to sort anything into them
Classification is a label on the information itself, wherever it travels: paper, folder or screen
Public: what it means and an everyday example; internal: meaning, example and handling; confidential: meaning, example and handling
The viewer sorts a few real everyday items into the three classes before the answer is shown
What to do when unsure: treat it as the higher class and ask
Back to the opening file, now classified and handled correctly

must_cover.what: The three classes are public, internal and confidential
Public: information approved for anyone outside the organisation, with a real everyday example
Internal: for employees only, low harm if disclosed, with a real everyday example
Confidential: limited to people who need it, real harm if disclosed, with a real everyday example
Each class sets how the item is handled and shared
When unsure, treat information as the higher class and ask the owner

must_avoid: Statistics or breach figures without a source
Naming specific laws, fines or regulators unless the knowledge sheet grounds them
Invented statements attributed to real people
Fear-led tone or threats of discipline
Opening by explaining what a term means, or with an agenda
A fourth class or company-specific tool names not in the knowledge sheet
example_posture: Ordinary office artefacts the viewer handled this week: a published press release or job ad, a team meeting note or org chart, a payroll file or customer list. One running example (a file someone is about to share) returns through the lesson.
visual_direction: Clean monoline outlines on white: documents, folders and screens drawn as single-line shapes whose outline colour marks the class, the same colour for a class every time. One object sorted at a time; the rule large when it is the point; the opening file seen again at the end.
voice_note: A calm, capable colleague explaining how things work here; plain, brief, never alarmist or preachy.
open_questions: No company policy document was supplied: the lesson describes a common three-tier scheme from the knowledge sheet; if the organisation has its own policy, its meanings and handling rules should replace these.
Who the 'owner' to ask is (manager, data owner, security team) depends on the organisation; the lesson will stay generic unless told.
